item.title: Random Article Review #11, 21 October 2016
item.content:encoded:
Wondertainment items follow a certain formula1, which has evolved over time, but largely proceeds along the "well-meaning but comically dangerous children's product, accompanied by a 'HEY KIDS' explanatory note" track. Whatever novelty this form may have had in earlier days, it's made the exercise kind of rote and tiresome after dozens of attempts at it, both extant and deleted.

The really funny thing to me is that this article has become sort of an ideal form of that exercise. Even if it were brand-new and posted today, I suspect that this would meet largely the same reaction that it did back in the day. Here's what this does right:

  • Captures the fundamental alien-ness of Doctor Wondertainment, an entity that would conceive completely without malice that something like this is appropriate for use as a children's toy
  • Has painstaking internal consistency, something that a lot of writers seem to equate with layering on of extraneous details until readers can't keep the whole thing straight
  • Actually sells the explanatory note correctly, treating it as an opportunity to shed some narrative on the object rather than just serving as a rote "HEY KIDS HERE'S WHAT THIS IS OK BYE"
  • Believably details the difficulty that something like this would present in containing it, the somewhat goofy reference to one researcher looking at the boobs of another notwithstanding
  • Uses puns in a way that isn't completely stupid and contrived

I have a lot of longstanding issues with Wondertainment, which in most cases I've found to be a lazily palette-swapped Willy Wonka for the SCPverse, but this is a good example of something being entertaining and well-written enough to overcome clashing preferences.

Footnotes
1. The Little Misters being their own thing, which I'll expound upon when this series inevitably reaches one of those articles.

item.content:encoded:
It ends the world. In fact, it's so apocalyptic, that it honestly breaks my suspension of disbelief that it hasn't ended the world yet. If you think about this wrong, it breaches containment. Of course, that's besides the point, because there's already other instances out there (remember, this is a made SCP, not something naturally occurring), some of which are in the hands of the very not-sanity-friendly Dr. Wondertainment (or, at least, the company).

It's basically only a matter of time until one of these appears in the hands of every child in the world, because Dr. Wondertainment wants his products to be enjoyed by all the little children. At this point, the world ends, because with that many people, someone's bound to think something apocalyptic. And there's nothing the Foundation, or anyone else, can do to stop this.

As I said, this is so dangerous it breaks suspension of disbelief.

I can't remember the name of the comic, but a few decades ago Phil Foglio did a short feature about how the Platonic ideals would come into being, then survive the end and new beginning of the Universe. The problem began with Winslow. It's a sentient (at least passably so) stuffed toy crocodile just under a meter long. The problem arises because different groups consider Winslow differently. Everyone seems to understand in one way or another that he's (it's?) a Platonic ideal. The problem is, what is he an ideal of? Is it stuffed crocodiles, stuffed animals, children's toys or sentient life?

Such quandries. I love stuff like this.

a single plus, added to the total. Could it be the Ideal Plus? I do not know.

item.content:encoded: I love this, and the puns, and Wondertainment, but for whatever reason this just feels wrong to me. It doesn't really match up with (what I understand of) Plato's views of true forms. After all, if this object represents the properties of the ideal 6-ball, would it not then also be able to be used and manipulated like a 6-ball (because if we could make it move with our minds it would no longer be ideal for competition)? It just seems like you wanted to insert Plato's theory into an SCP and built around it into something readable and entertaining (which it certainly is). Like I said, this is really great and really well written, but I'll have to downvote. Then again, who am I to talk?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
As I commented in chat, this is far too uncontained and apocalyptic to not be Keter. If anyone thinks the wrong thing while looking at it, the world ends. Certainly, outside of containment, it's hard to bring back into containment, because one idle thought can cause it to duplicate to anywhere.

We know instances exist outside of containment, because it's made by Dr. Wondertainment. It's pretty easy to imagine Wondertainment looking at one of these and thinking how great it would be for every child in the world to have one. Hell, it would almost be out of character for him not to think that. And then the world ends.

Setting aside the implausibility of this not already having destroyed the world, there's a couple other issues. I don't feel like Descartes should be trademarked, seeing as the other philosopher puns aren't, and it doesn't really add anything to make it trademarked. I'm not positive if I see this as a Wondertainment object; it feels a bit too abstract. But if you do want it to be Wondertainment, the assembly booklet should not be in 6-point type. That's not very child friendly. Instead it should be printed in 14-point comic sans filling a hundred or so pages.
